doc.title: Bernie Kirsh interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 27, 2022

chapter: Music beginnings and entering the studio
title: From technical theater to the Bitter End and Electric Lady
summary: Kirsh moved from theater and campus television to running lights and sound at the Bitter End, then began watching sessions at Jimi Hendrix's studio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah. But at some point did you start hearing ways of recording music that you noticed and then what made you enter this world?

Happenstance. I had no interest — well back up a little bit. When I was in college I actually turned into a theater major and got involved in technical theater, did all the other things that a theater student would do — acting, directing, and so forth. But then got an offer for a graduate assistantship in technical theater: building sets and that sort of thing. So I went to graduate school doing that and while I was there I got involved in the television station at the school. And of course I had my theater background and I understood, started to understand lighting and all those aspects. Sound was always the poor cousin. It never got its due. So I really didn’t have much attention on sound, and no interest in it really. But then after college, after grad school I went to New York to want to work in television. So I’m staying with a friend in an apartment in Greenwich Village on Bleecker Street and right down the street was The Bitter End, which was a mainstream club in those days. This was 1970. And it was there that I heard there was an opening from somebody, for doing the lights and sound. And I knew about lighting. Didn’t know anything about sound. So I took the job and did that for about a year or so. And there would be recordings that would go on there. Live recordings. Curtis Mayfield, all these great artists just coming through there. I mean there would be Carly Simon opening for Kris Kristofferson, you know it was that era, but major acts. So the people who would come in to record were of some experience and they would park a truck outside. So one day an engineer came in who was doing the recording and we started talking and this and that, and he mentioned that Jimi Hendrix had opened up a studio around the corner and that’s where he was working. And I said, “Oh can I come watch?” Be kind of interesting © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

you know. And so I went over there every day for a couple of weeks. I was working nights of course, at the club, and during the day I would just go over there and spend hours just sitting in the back of the room watching what was going on, and got interested. I got interested in the process, in working with musicians, which I had been doing at the club, but I love musicians. And you know it’s my group, my people. And so it was a way for me to interact with them. I wasn’t playing anymore, I really wasn’t playing the horn anymore, I was really involved more in the service activities around music.
